hits.full_text:
Who are your roots?

This idea from Tyler Perry that changed my life…

There are three types of people in your life:

Leaves: These are the people that are only around from time to time when the weather is good. They blow around as the winds change. They provide shade during the summer, but as soon as winter comes, they fall off the tree and disappear.

Branches: These are the people who are more present and stable than the leaves, but they aren’t permanent. They look strong, but if you try to stand on them or pull yourself up from them, they may break under your weight.

Roots: These are the people who are permanent. They are deep and wide. They are there in the summer and the winter, they are unperturbed by the changing seasons. The leaves and branches may come and go, but the roots are there forever.

I love this perspective.

There’s nothing wrong with having leaves and branches in your life. When times are good, they can bring joy to your world. But never make the mistake of thinking they will be there during the bad.

The most important question:

Who are your roots?

Who are the people who will be there through good and bad?

Who are the people who will sit in the mud with you?

Find them. Cherish them. Be a root to someone else.
hits.hook: Bloom: leaves, branches, roots (Tyler Perry); who are your roots?
hits.draft_en:
Who's still around in the slow months? Not the people who show up for good news. The ones who sit with you when there isn't any.

If one comes to mind, this might be a good week to tell them.

patterns: Subtraction is the theme: Ferriss 'separate the critical few from the trivial many' (~46.4k) and his Ramit quote 'invest 10x more in one or two areas' (fresh, 2 replies). Softened for the brand into: two things done with attention, the rest let go.
Use what's in front of you: Clear's 'use what you already know' (~49.8k, 322 saves, replies locked). The analog version is the notebook already on the desk, not a better method.
Question hooks lead: 'Who are your roots?', 'Should you specialize or be a generalist?', 'What would it look like to…'. Bloom's roots post opens and closes on the same question.
Three-type metaphors: Bloom's leaves, branches, roots (~33.1k). People sorted by who stays in winter. Keep it gentle; no cutting people off.
Patience as the work: Bloom's 'outlast uncertainty' (~6.9k in 15 minutes, 21 replies). Brand angle: nothing looks like it's happening for a long time, and that counts.

Outsiders: 'believed in me' is everywhere (milestone thank-yous, sports, music); 'small steps, big results' is bot-saturated and worth avoiding word for word. Analog craft (hand-turned fountain pens) and burnout-prevention posts are the quieter threads.

Still climbing from yesterday: Bloom's 'people who believed in you early' 13.3k to ~207.6k (8.6k likes) and Ferriss's depression practices 33.4k to ~66.1k (1,200 saves). Save-heavy, practical posts keep winning.

reply_ideas.reply_text: Outlasting it is mostly unglamorous. Same desk, same small next step, no new information for longer than feels reasonable. I think that's why so few people stay for it.
The other half of that question is what you quietly stop doing to make room. That list is usually longer, and harder to write, than the one about where to invest.
Where I keep landing: be a generalist about what you read and a specialist about what you finish. Curious whether that holds up against what you found.
The winter test is a good one. The roots are rarely the loudest people around, and they never need you to have good news before they show up.
